description:
Could You Survive Jumping From the Edge of Space?

In 2012 Felix Baumgartner jumped from about 39 km up and broke the speed of sound in free fall. In 2014 Alan Eustace jumped from over 41 km. Here is what that fall is really like.

Follow for daily trips through the universe. 🚀

Images: NASA, ESA, ESO and Wikimedia Commons (free licenses, credited in the video file's notes)
Narration: AI voice

#spacejump #space #science #astronomy #shorts #science

segments.text: Could you jump from the edge of space, and survive?
In 2012, a skydiver rode a balloon up to about thirty-nine kilometers, more than three times higher than a passenger jet.
The air up there is so thin that your blood would boil without a pressure suit.
segments.headline: You need a pressure suit

segments.text: He stepped off, and with almost no air to slow him down, he fell faster than the speed of sound.
He went into a dangerous spin, but got control, and opened his parachute safely.
segments.headline: A deadly spin

segments.text: Two years later, a Google executive named Alan Eustace jumped from over forty-one kilometers.
But real space starts at about a hundred kilometers. From orbit, you'd be moving sideways too fast to just fall. You'd need a heat shield.
segments.headline: Space is higher

segments.text: Next stop: TRAPPIST-1. Would you ever do this jump? Yes or no in the comments, and follow for the next stop.
